overview: Embedding is Go's mechanism for composition: you declare a type (struct or interface) as an anonymous field inside another type, and the outer type gains the embedded type's fields and methods 'for free' via promotion.

Embedding is composition, NOT inheritance — there is no base/derived class hierarchy, no constructors chaining, and crucially no virtual dispatch: an embedded method that calls another method always calls the embedded type's own methods, never an overriding method on the outer type.

Two flavors exist: struct embedding (anonymous struct/pointer fields whose members get promoted) and interface embedding (composing a larger interface from smaller ones, or embedding an interface in a struct to build wrappers/decorators).
learningObjectives: Declare anonymous (embedded) fields in structs and interfaces and explain how field and method promotion populates the outer type's method set.
Access the embedded value explicitly by its type name (e.g. `outer.Base.Field`) and apply the shadowing rules when names collide.
Compose interfaces by embedding (io.ReadWriteCloser) and embed an interface inside a struct to build a decorator/wrapper that overrides one method and delegates the rest.
Articulate why embedding gives NO polymorphism/virtual dispatch and avoid the Java-style 'override the base method' mistake.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: Embedding is the inclusion of a type as an anonymous field in a struct or interface; the embedded type's exported and unexported fields and methods are promoted to the embedding type, becoming part of its method set and selector namespace unless shadowed by a member declared at a shallower depth.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: When you write a struct field with a type but no name (e.g. `type User struct { Logger }`), Go treats `Logger`'s fields and methods as if they belonged directly to `User`. You can call `user.Log(...)` even though `Log` is defined on `Logger`. It looks like inheritance but it is really 'has-a' composition with automatic forwarding.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Go's designers (Pike, Thompson, Griesemer) deliberately rejected classical inheritance after years of fragile-base-class and deep-hierarchy problems in C++ and Java. Embedding, introduced with the language in 2009 and described in 'Effective Go', delivers code reuse through composition while keeping types flat. It pairs with Go's structural interfaces: a type satisfies an interface implicitly, and embedding lets it inherit that satisfaction from a member.

whyItMatters.business: Composition keeps codebases flat and refactorable, so teams ship features faster without untangling deep class hierarchies that slow every change.
whyItMatters.engineering: Embedding removes boilerplate delegation code — you reuse a Logger, a sync.Mutex, or a base entity without hand-writing forwarding methods, reducing bugs and review surface.
whyItMatters.scalability: Decorator/wrapper patterns built on embedding (middleware, instrumented clients) let large systems add cross-cutting behavior without modifying or duplicating the wrapped implementations.
whyItMatters.cost: Less duplicated forwarding code means fewer lines to maintain and test, lowering long-term engineering cost.
whyItMatters.reliability: Because embedding is composition with explicit method sets (no hidden virtual dispatch), behavior is predictable and statically checkable, avoiding a whole class of fragile-base-class surprises.

coreComponents.name: Embedded (anonymous) field
coreComponents.definition: A struct field declared with only a type and no field name, e.g. `Logger` inside `type User struct { Logger }`.
coreComponents.purpose: Splice another type's members into the outer type for reuse.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Hold the embedded value and expose its members for promotion; it is accessible by its type name (user.Logger).
coreComponents.examples: type User struct { Base; Name string }

coreComponents.name: Promoted field
coreComponents.definition: A field of the embedded type made directly accessible on the outer type as if declared there.
coreComponents.purpose: Read/write embedded data without naming the embedded type.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Resolve `outer.X` to `outer.Embedded.X` when X exists only on the embedded type at the shallowest depth.
coreComponents.examples: user.ID where ID lives on the embedded Base

coreComponents.name: Promoted method
coreComponents.definition: A method of the embedded type added to the outer type's method set.
coreComponents.purpose: Let the outer type satisfy interfaces and be called as if it owned the method.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Forward `outer.M()` to the embedded receiver `outer.Embedded.M()` automatically.

coreComponents.name: Embedded interface
coreComponents.definition: An interface listed by name inside another interface or as an anonymous field of a struct.
coreComponents.purpose: Compose larger interfaces (io.ReadWriteCloser) or satisfy an interface in a struct while overriding only some methods.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Contribute its method set to the union; in a struct it supplies a stored implementation to delegate to.
coreComponents.examples: type ReadWriteCloser interface { Reader; Writer; Closer }

coreComponents.name: Shadowing (outer member)
coreComponents.definition: A field or method declared directly on the outer type with the same name as a promoted one.
coreComponents.purpose: Let the outer type override or specialize the embedded behavior at the call site.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Win selector resolution at depth 0, hiding the embedded member of the same name.

coreComponents.name: Outer (embedding) type
coreComponents.definition: The struct or interface that contains the anonymous field.
coreComponents.purpose: Compose and extend the embedded type's capabilities.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Own the embedded value, expose promoted members, and may add or shadow members.

internalWorking: At compile time the embedded type is stored as a real field whose field name equals the unqualified type name (Logger embeds as a field literally named `Logger`, `*bytes.Buffer` as `Buffer`).

The compiler computes the outer type's method set by walking embedded fields breadth-first; each promoted method becomes a thin forwarding wrapper that calls the method on the embedded field with the appropriate receiver.
Selector resolution `x.f` searches for f at the shallowest embedding depth; a unique shallowest match wins, the outer type's own member (depth 0) always wins over any promoted one.

If two embedded types provide the same name at the SAME depth and you select it without qualification, the program fails to compile with an 'ambiguous selector' error — you must disambiguate (x.A.f or x.B.f).

Method-set promotion respects receivers: embedding a value `Base` promotes Base's value-receiver methods to the outer value and both value/pointer methods to the outer pointer; embedding `*Base` promotes all of Base's methods because you always have a pointer.

There is no vtable linking embedded methods back to the outer type: when a promoted method M internally calls N, it dispatches statically to the embedded type's N, NOT to any N the outer type declares — this is the absence of virtual dispatch.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: source: type Outer struct { Embedded } --compile--> [Embedded stored as field named 'Embedded'] --> [method-set computed by BFS over embeds] --> selector outer.M --> [shallowest unique match? outer's own M wins over promoted; tie at same depth => compile error] --> promoted call forwards to outer.Embedded.M(receiver = outer.Embedded)
dataFlowWalkthrough: You declare `type User struct { Base; Name string }` where Base has field ID and method Describe().
The compiler records Base as a field named `Base`, then promotes ID and Describe() onto User's namespace and method set.
Calling `u.Describe()` resolves to `u.Base.Describe()` with the receiver being u.Base, not u.
Reading `u.ID` resolves to `u.Base.ID`; assigning `u.ID = 5` writes through to the embedded value.

If User also declares its own `Describe()`, that depth-0 method shadows Base's, so `u.Describe()` now calls User's version — but any code inside Base that calls Describe still calls Base.Describe (no callback into User).

keyTerminology.meaning: Including a type as an anonymous field in a struct or interface.
keyTerminology.importance: The core composition mechanism; the whole topic.

keyTerminology.meaning: Making an embedded type's fields/methods accessible directly on the outer type.
keyTerminology.importance: Explains why outer.M() works without redeclaring M.

keyTerminology.meaning: The set of methods callable on a type (and thus which interfaces it satisfies).
keyTerminology.importance: Embedding grows the method set, enabling interface satisfaction by composition.

keyTerminology.meaning: An outer (shallower) member hiding a promoted member of the same name.
keyTerminology.importance: Governs override-like behavior and selector resolution.

keyTerminology.meaning: A name provided by two embeds at the same depth, unselectable without qualification.
keyTerminology.importance: A compile error you must disambiguate; common collision pitfall.

keyTerminology.meaning: Dynamic dispatch to an overriding method based on runtime type.
keyTerminology.importance: Go embedding does NOT have it — the key difference from inheritance.

importantConcepts.explanation: An embedded field is a real 'has-a' relationship: User HAS a Base, it is not a subclass of Base. The outer type can be used anywhere the embedded methods are needed, but there is no type hierarchy and no is-a substitutability beyond satisfied interfaces.

There is no `super.Method()` and no callback from embedded code into outer overrides. If you shadow Base.M with Outer.M, you call the embedded version explicitly via outer.Base.M(); Base's internal calls to M never reach Outer.M.

importantConcepts.concept: Embedding an interface in a struct = stored implementation
importantConcepts.explanation: Putting `io.Reader` as an anonymous struct field means the struct satisfies Reader by delegating to whatever Reader value you store, letting you override Read while delegating all other methods of a larger interface — the decorator/wrapper pattern.

importantConcepts.concept: Pointer vs value embedding affects method set and sharing
importantConcepts.explanation: Embedding `*Base` shares one Base instance and promotes all its methods; embedding `Base` copies it and promotes only value-receiver methods to the outer value. Choose based on mutation, nil-handling, and method receivers.

variationsAndTypes: Struct value embedding: `type User struct { Base }` — Base copied by value, both share zero-value-ready semantics.
Struct pointer embedding: `type User struct { *Base }` — shares one Base, but the pointer can be nil and panic when a promoted method is called.
Interface composition: `type ReadWriteCloser interface { Reader; Writer; Closer }` — union of method sets, no implementation.
Interface-in-struct (decorator/wrapper): `type LoggingConn struct { net.Conn }` — embed the interface to satisfy it while overriding select methods and delegating the rest.
Multiple embedding: embedding several types at once, with collision rules deciding promotion.
Embedding standard-library mixins: sync.Mutex, sync.RWMutex, or sync.WaitGroup embedded to add locking to a struct.
advantages: Eliminates hand-written delegation boilerplate — promoted methods/fields are automatic.
Enables interface satisfaction by composition (the outer type inherits the embedded type's satisfied interfaces).
Powers clean decorator/middleware/wrapper patterns by embedding an interface and overriding one method.
Keeps types flat and refactorable, avoiding deep fragile hierarchies.
Lets you add cross-cutting concerns (mutexes, loggers) with one line.
disadvantages: No polymorphism/virtual dispatch — embedded methods cannot call back into outer overrides, surprising those expecting inheritance.
Name collisions at the same depth cause compile errors and must be disambiguated.
Promotion can unintentionally expose embedded methods/fields, widening the API or breaking encapsulation.
Pointer embedding can panic on nil; value embedding silently copies, which can cause stale-state bugs.
Method-set rules with pointer vs value embedding are subtle and easy to get wrong.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: When you want code reuse via composition, to satisfy an interface by delegating to a stored implementation, to build decorators/wrappers, or to mix in capabilities like locking or logging.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: When you actually need polymorphic override behavior (use explicit interfaces and method calls instead), or when promotion would leak internals — prefer a named field plus explicit, minimal delegation.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Embedding is like a manager who has an assistant on staff. When you ask the manager to 'schedule a meeting', the request is silently handled by the assistant (promotion) — you don't even know it was delegated. But if you teach the assistant a procedure that says 'call the office to confirm', the assistant always calls the ASSISTANT's own office contact, never the manager's newer contact, even if the manager later overrode that step. The manager can take a task back personally (shadowing), but the assistant's internal steps never magically route through the manager. That is composition with delegation, not a chain of command that calls upward.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Embedding is inheritance, so the outer type is a subclass of the embedded type.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It is composition ('has-a'); there is no class hierarchy and no is-a substitutability beyond interfaces the outer type satisfies.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Overriding a promoted method makes the embedded type's internal calls use my new version (virtual dispatch).
commonMisconceptions.reality: No. Embedded methods statically call the embedded type's own methods; there is no callback into the outer override and no `super`.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Embedding a pointer and embedding a value behave the same.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They differ in copying, nil-safety, and which receiver methods get promoted to the outer value's method set.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can't access the embedded value directly once embedded.
commonMisconceptions.reality: You can always reach it by its type name, e.g. user.Base.Field or conn.Conn.Close().

productionConsiderations.scalability: Decorator chains built by embedding interfaces (middleware, instrumented clients) compose cleanly, but keep chains shallow and avoid promoting methods you don't intend to expose.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Prefer value embedding or guarantee non-nil pointer embeds in constructors so promoted method calls never panic on a nil embedded pointer.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: When embedding an interface in a wrapper, ensure the embedded implementation is always set; a nil embedded interface makes every delegated call panic.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Wrappers that embed an interface are ideal seams for adding metrics/tracing around the one overridden method while delegating the rest unchanged.
productionConsiderations.security: Beware promotion leaking unexported-to-package or sensitive methods/fields into a wider API; embed deliberately and document the exposed surface.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Embedding replaces hand-written delegation, cutting maintenance cost; value-embedding small mixins (sync.Mutex) avoids extra allocations.
productionConsiderations.performance: Promoted method calls are thin static forwards with negligible overhead — no dynamic dispatch cost — so embedding is essentially free at runtime.

codeExamples.title: Struct embedding with field and method promotion
codeExamples.overview: Embed a Base struct (with a Logger mixin) into User and call promoted methods/fields directly, then access the embedded value by its type name.
codeExamples.breakdown: Logger is embedded in Base, and Base is embedded in User, so promotion chains: User gains ID, Prefix, and Log(). `u.ID` is shorthand for `u.Base.ID`; `u.Log(...)` forwards to `u.Base.Logger.Log(...)` with the receiver being the Logger value. The embedded fields are real fields named by their type (Base, Logger), so you can always write the explicit path `u.Base.Logger.Log(...)`. Promotion is purely syntactic forwarding — no inheritance is involved.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
ID: 7
[USER] created
Prefix: USER
via u.Base.ID: 99
[USER] explicit path
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting that the embedded field name is the bare type name (Base/Logger), so trying `u.base` (lowercase) fails. Also, initializing with a positional literal `User{Base{...}, "Ada"}` requires naming the embedded field in struct literals when mixing with named fields.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Embed small value mixins (Logger, sync.Mutex) by value to avoid an extra allocation and nil checks; only embed pointers when you must share or mutate one instance.

codeExamples.title: Embedding an interface to build a decorator/wrapper
codeExamples.overview: Compose io.ReadWriteCloser from smaller interfaces, then embed io.ReadCloser in a struct to override Read (uppercasing bytes) while delegating Close unchanged — the decorator pattern.
codeExamples.breakdown: The interface embedding `ReadWriteCloser { Reader; Writer; Closer }` simply unions the three method sets — no implementation, just a bigger contract. The decorator `upperReader` embeds the io.ReadCloser INTERFACE as a field: because a value is stored there, upperReader instantly satisfies io.ReadCloser, getting Read and Close 'for free'. We then declare our own Read, which shadows the promoted Read and delegates to `u.ReadCloser.Read` before transforming the bytes. Close is left untouched and is delegated to the wrapped value. This is the idiomatic Go way to wrap only part of a larger interface.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
HELLO GO
closed via promoted Close
codeExamples.commonIssues: Leaving the embedded interface field nil (e.g. `upperReader{}`) makes every delegated call panic with a nil-pointer dereference. Also, if you forget to delegate inside your override (calling some other reader), you break the contract.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Embed the smallest interface you actually wrap (io.ReadCloser, not io.ReadWriteCloser) so you only delegate what you need and don't claim methods you can't honor.

codeExamples.title: Shadowing and the absence of virtual dispatch
codeExamples.overview: Demonstrate that an outer method shadows the promoted one, and prove there is NO callback into the outer override from embedded code (no Java-style virtual dispatch).
codeExamples.breakdown: Dog embeds Animal and declares its own Sound, which shadows the promoted Animal.Sound, so `d.Sound()` prints 'Woof'. But `d.Describe()` is the promoted Animal.Describe; inside it, `a.Sound()` binds to Animal.Sound at compile time because the receiver is the Animal value, not the Dog. There is no vtable redirecting that call to Dog.Sound — hence 'Rex says ...' rather than 'Rex says Woof'. This is the single most important contrast with classical inheritance: embedding has no virtual dispatch and no `super`. If you genuinely need overridable behavior, model it with an interface and pass the value as that interface, or have Dog define its own Describe.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
d.Sound(): Woof
d.Describe(): Rex says ...
d.Animal.Sound(): ...
explicit override result: Rex says Woof
codeExamples.commonIssues: Expecting `d.Describe()` to print 'Rex says Woof' (Java-style override). It does not, because Go embedding is composition without virtual dispatch.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: When you truly need overriding, define an interface (e.g. Sounder) and have the calling code accept it; then each concrete type's Sound is dispatched dynamically through the interface, which is Go's substitute for virtual methods.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A payments service must add structured request logging and per-call latency metrics to an existing HTTP client without modifying the client and without losing any of its many methods.
endToEndExample.inputData: An *http.Client-like dependency exposed as a Doer interface { Do(*http.Request) (*http.Response, error) } plus the requests flowing through the service.
endToEndExample.architecture: An instrumentedClient struct embeds the Doer interface (so it satisfies Doer automatically by delegation) and overrides only Do() to wrap timing and logging around the embedded implementation — a decorator built with interface embedding.
processingSteps: Define `type instrumentedClient struct { Doer; log *slog.Logger }`, embedding the interface so all Doer methods are promoted.
Override Do(): record start time, call `c.Doer.Do(req)` to delegate, then log method, URL, status, and elapsed time.
Construct it as `instrumentedClient{Doer: realClient, log: logger}` so the embedded interface is never nil.
Inject the wrapper anywhere a Doer is expected; callers are unchanged.
endToEndExample.output: Every outbound request now emits a structured log line with latency, while all behavior of the underlying client is preserved unchanged via delegation.
endToEndExample.monitoring: The overridden Do() is the single seam where you emit metrics (histogram of latency, counter by status code) and trace spans.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Do() delegates to the embedded Doer, logs the error if non-nil, and returns it unchanged; the constructor guarantees the embedded Doer is non-nil so delegation never panics.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Cross-cutting observability is added with about a dozen lines and zero changes to the underlying client, because interface embedding promoted every other method while letting us override just Do().

industryUseCases.problem: Expose composite IO contracts without redefining methods.
industryUseCases.solution: io.ReadWriteCloser and friends are defined purely by embedding io.Reader, io.Writer, and io.Closer.
industryUseCases.benefits: Smaller interfaces compose into larger ones with zero boilerplate and clear semantics.

industryUseCases.problem: Many API objects share common metadata and need consistent accessors.
industryUseCases.solution: Types embed metav1.TypeMeta and metav1.ObjectMeta so every object promotes the same metadata fields and methods.
industryUseCases.benefits: Uniform object structure and reuse across hundreds of resource types without duplication.

industryUseCases.problem: Service implementations must stay forward-compatible as new RPCs are added.
industryUseCases.solution: Generated code provides UnimplementedXxxServer structs that users embed, promoting default method stubs.
industryUseCases.benefits: Adding RPCs doesn't break existing servers because the embedded stub supplies defaults via promotion.

industryUseCases.problem: Add logging, auth, and metrics around handlers and response writers without rewriting them.
industryUseCases.solution: Wrappers embed http.ResponseWriter (an interface) and override WriteHeader to capture the status code while delegating the rest.
industryUseCases.benefits: Decorators add cross-cutting behavior transparently while preserving the full ResponseWriter contract.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Decorator chains built on interface embedding (logging -> metrics -> retry -> transport) scale behavior additively; keep each layer single-purpose and the embedded interface minimal so the chain stays comprehensible.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Always initialize embedded interface fields in constructors; a nil embedded interface turns every delegated call into a panic, so make non-nil an invariant and fail fast at construction.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Wrappers that embed interfaces are the natural place to add timeouts, circuit breakers, and retries around the delegated call without touching the wrapped implementation, improving resilience.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Because embedding is static composition, swapping the embedded implementation (e.g. a fallback client) is a one-line change in the constructor, easing failover configuration.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Promoted method calls are thin static forwards with no dynamic dispatch overhead; embed by value for tiny mixins to avoid pointer indirection and extra allocations on hot paths.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Embedding eliminates hand-written delegation methods, reducing code volume, test surface, and maintenance cost across large object hierarchies.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Promotion can inadvertently widen a type's public API by exposing embedded methods/fields; embed only what you intend to expose and review the resulting method set, especially when embedding third-party types.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: The single overridden method in a decorator is the ideal instrumentation seam — emit metrics, logs, and trace spans there while delegating the core work to the embedded value.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: When overriding a promoted method, validate inputs/outputs in the override and then delegate, ensuring the wrapped implementation still receives well-formed data.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Embed a logger mixin or wrap via interface embedding to attach consistent structured logging; alert on the panic rate that a nil embedded interface would produce.

recommendedPractices: Use embedding for composition and reuse, not to simulate inheritance — never expect virtual dispatch.
Embed the smallest interface you actually need to wrap when building decorators.
Initialize embedded pointer/interface fields in constructors so promoted calls never panic.
Access the embedded value explicitly (outer.Base.X) when you need the un-shadowed member.
Embed standard mixins like sync.Mutex by value to add capabilities cleanly.
engineeringStandards: Review the outer type's resulting method set to ensure promotion doesn't leak unintended API.
Disambiguate same-depth name collisions explicitly rather than relying on accidental resolution.
Prefer composition with an explicit named field plus minimal delegation when you must hide most of a type's surface.
designRecommendations: Model overridable/polymorphic behavior with interfaces, not by shadowing promoted methods.
Keep embedding shallow; deep promotion chains hurt readability and complicate collision rules.
When wrapping, override only the method(s) that need new behavior and delegate the rest.
namingConventions: Refer to embedded values by their type name in code paths that need the explicit member (conn.Conn.Close()).
Name decorator types after the behavior they add (loggingTransport, instrumentedClient), not after the wrapped type.
documentationStandards: Document which methods a wrapper overrides versus delegates.
Note when a type embeds another and call out any shadowed members and their intended semantics.
testingStrategies: Assert that the outer type satisfies the intended interface with a compile-time check: `var _ io.ReadCloser = upperReader{}`.
Test that overridden methods delegate correctly (spy/mock the embedded interface).
Add a test proving no-virtual-dispatch expectations so future readers don't reintroduce the inheritance assumption.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting an overridden promoted method to be called from embedded code (Java-style virtual dispatch).
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Mental model carried over from class-based inheritance.
commonMistakes.impact: Embedded methods silently call the embedded type's own methods, producing 'wrong' results that look like a logic bug.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use interfaces for polymorphism; have callers depend on the interface so the concrete method dispatches dynamically.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaving an embedded interface (or pointer) field nil.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Constructing the wrapper with a zero-value literal and forgetting to set the embedded field.
commonMistakes.impact: Every delegated/promoted call panics with a nil-pointer dereference.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Always set the embedded field in a constructor and enforce the non-nil invariant.

commonMistakes.mistake: Triggering an ambiguous selector by embedding two types with a same-named member.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Two embeds promote the same field/method at the same depth.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Qualify the access (outer.A.X or outer.B.X) or declare an outer member that shadows both.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming pointer and value embedding are interchangeable.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Not understanding receiver/method-set rules and copy semantics.
commonMistakes.impact: Unexpected copies (stale state) with value embedding, or nil panics and shared mutation with pointer embedding.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Embed by value for small immutable mixins; embed by pointer only to share/mutate one instance and ensure it's non-nil.

comparisonSection.explanation: Embedding is 'has-a' with automatic delegation and NO virtual dispatch/super; inheritance is 'is-a' with overridable methods and a base/derived hierarchy. Go deliberately has only the former.
A shadowing outer method wins only for direct calls; embedded code still calls the embedded method. Inheritance redirects base calls to overrides via a vtable.
Embedding promotes everything automatically (less code, less control over exposure); an explicit field with hand-written forwarding gives precise control over which methods you expose.

Value embedding copies the instance and promotes only value-receiver methods to the outer value; pointer embedding shares one instance, promotes all methods, but can be nil and panic on promoted calls.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is embedding in Go and is it inheritance?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Embedding is declaring a type as an anonymous field so its fields/methods are promoted to the outer type. It is composition, not inheritance.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Tests the core mental model that Go uses 'has-a' composition.

beginnerQuestions.question: How do you access an embedded value explicitly?
beginnerQuestions.answer: By its type name, e.g. outer.Base.Field or conn.Conn.Close().
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Confirms the candidate knows the embedded field is named after its type.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is method/field promotion and how does selector resolution handle name collisions?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Promotion exposes embedded members on the outer type. Resolution picks the shallowest unique match; an outer (depth-0) member shadows promoted ones, and two members at the same depth cause an ambiguous-selector compile error.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Tests understanding of shadowing and ambiguity rules.

intermediateQuestions.question: How does embedding let a type satisfy an interface?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Promoted methods join the outer type's method set, so if an embedded type's methods cover an interface, the outer type satisfies it automatically — including embedding an interface value in a struct.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Links embedding to Go's structural interface satisfaction.

advancedQuestions.question: Does embedding provide virtual dispatch? Show with an example.
advancedQuestions.answer: No. If Base.Describe calls Base.Sound and Outer shadows Sound, Outer.Describe (promoted) still calls Base.Sound, not Outer.Sound. There is no super and no vtable redirect.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Tests the critical no-virtual-dispatch insight and the inheritance contrast.

advancedQuestions.question: How do pointer vs value embedding differ in method sets and runtime behavior?
advancedQuestions.answer: Embedding *Base promotes all of Base's methods (you always have a pointer) and shares one instance but can be nil; embedding Base copies it and promotes only value-receiver methods to the outer value, with pointer-receiver methods available on *Outer.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: You wrap an http.ResponseWriter to capture the status code, but after wrapping, calls to Hijack/Flush stop working even though you only overrode WriteHeader.
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Embedding the ResponseWriter interface promotes only the methods in that interface; optional methods like Hijacker/Flusher are separate interfaces that your wrapper no longer exposes unless it forwards them.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Embed http.ResponseWriter so Write/Header/WriteHeader delegate, override WriteHeader to capture status, and explicitly implement Hijack/Flush by type-asserting and forwarding to the embedded writer to preserve those optional interfaces.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a layered, instrumented HTTP transport (logging, metrics, retries) without modifying the underlying transport.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Define an interface (e.g. http.RoundTripper), and create decorator structs that each embed the interface and override RoundTrip to add one concern while delegating to the embedded next layer.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Embedding gives free delegation and clean layering but no virtual dispatch, so cross-layer overriding must be modeled via the interface; deep chains can obscure ordering.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Compose layers in a fixed order behind a constructor, keep each layer single-purpose, and make the embedded interface non-nil to avoid panics as the chain grows.

followUpQuestions: How would you preserve optional interfaces (Flusher, Hijacker) when wrapping http.ResponseWriter?
When is manual delegation with a named field better than embedding?
How does embedding interact with json struct tags and field promotion during marshaling?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Embedding is composition via anonymous fields: the embedded type's fields and methods are promoted to the outer type, with no inheritance and no virtual dispatch.
keyConcepts: Anonymous field = type with no field name; its name IS the type name.
Promotion exposes embedded fields/methods on the outer type.
Outer member shadows promoted member; same-depth tie = ambiguous selector error.
Interface embedding composes method sets; embedding an interface in a struct builds decorators.
No virtual dispatch: embedded methods call the embedded type's own methods.
formulas: outer.X resolves to outer.<Embedded>.X at the shallowest unique depth (depth-0 wins).
MethodSet(Outer) = own methods ∪ promoted methods from embeds (receiver rules apply).
commands: go vet ./...                                  // catches some embedding/shadowing issues
go doc <type>                                 // shows promoted methods in the method set
interviewPoints: Promotion grows the method set and can satisfy interfaces.
Shadowing is static; there is no super and no virtual dispatch.
Pointer vs value embedding changes method set, copying, and nil-safety.
quickNotes: Reach the embedded value via its type name: outer.Base.Field.
Embed the smallest interface when wrapping; delegate the rest.
Nil embedded interface/pointer => panic on promoted calls.
Use interfaces, not shadowing, when you need polymorphism.

keyTakeaways: Embedding is composition through anonymous fields: the embedded type's fields and methods are promoted to the outer type, eliminating delegation boilerplate.
It is NOT inheritance — there is no base/derived hierarchy, no super, and no virtual dispatch; embedded methods always call the embedded type's own methods even when the outer type shadows them.

Interface embedding composes larger interfaces (io.ReadWriteCloser) and, when embedded in a struct, lets you build decorators that override one method while delegating the rest to a stored implementation.
Mind the rules: outer members shadow promoted ones, same-depth collisions are compile errors, and pointer vs value embedding changes method sets, copying, and nil-safety.
